title: Finance & Financial Modelling
summary: P3 teaches the finance you need at work and at home, in Excel: loans and EMIs, investment decisions, accounts, budgets, and a full three-statement model with a DCF valuation.
prereq: Builds on C1 · Excel Foundations and C2 · Formulas & Functions. P1’s what-if tools (data tables, Goal Seek) come back in Modules 2 and 9.
outcomes: Use Excel’s time-value functions (FV, PV, PMT, NPER, RATE) with the right signs and periods.
Build loan EMI and amortisation schedules, and compare loan offers on their true cost.
Appraise investments with NPV, IRR, XNPV, XIRR, payback and MIRR.
Turn transactions into a trial balance and financial statements, with depreciation and ratios.
Build driver-based budgets and forecasts, and explain variances.
Lay out models to professional standards: inputs, calculations, outputs and checks.
Build a linked three-statement model and value a business with a DCF.
Test a model with scenarios, sensitivity tables, Goal Seek and Solver, and present the results.

lessons.title: NPV and the discount rate
lessons.summary: An investment is money out now for money back later. Discount every year’s cash flow to today and add them up: if the net present value is above zero, the project earns more than the return you require.
objectives: Lay out a project as yearly cash flows, with year 0 for the money spent now.
Discount each cash flow and add them up to get the NPV.

modules.title: Budgets and forecasts
modules.summary: A driver-based budget, monthly phasing with seasonality, budget versus actual with price and volume variances, and rolling forecasts.

lessons.title: A driver-based budget
lessons.summary: A budget is the year’s plan in numbers. Build it from drivers (volumes, prices, costs per unit, fixed costs) rather than last year plus 10%, and every line explains itself and changes when a driver does.
objectives: Say what a budget is for and who uses it.
Build revenue and material costs from volume, price and cost per unit.
Treat costs as variable, fixed or a % of revenue.
Turn the drivers into a budget P&L, and work out what a change in one driver does.
topics: Keep the drivers in one place

lessons.title: Monthly phasing and seasonality
lessons.summary: A yearly budget is phased into months so it can be tracked. Seasonality weights spread sales the way they really fall (Diwali high, monsoon low); variable costs follow sales, fixed costs spread evenly.
objectives: Explain why a budget is phased by month.
Work out seasonality weights from last year’s monthly sales.
Phase revenue and variable costs by the weights, and fixed costs evenly.
Check that the months add back to the year, and spot the weak months.
topics: Why phase the budget by month?
Phase each line the right way

lessons.title: Budget versus actual
lessons.summary: Each month, compare actual results with the budget. The variance is actual minus budget; whether it’s good news depends on the line. Split a sales variance into price and volume to see what really happened.
objectives: Work out variances in rupees and as a percentage of budget.
Label each variance favourable or adverse, depending on whether the line is income or a cost.
Split a revenue variance into volume and price.
Decide which variances deserve a question, and why.

lessons.title: Rolling forecasts
lessons.summary: The budget stays fixed; the forecast moves. Each month, combine the actuals so far with a fresh forecast for the rest of the year to get the full-year outlook. A run-rate keeps the seasonality; a straight-line trend can miss it.
objectives: Explain how a forecast differs from a budget.
Combine year-to-date actuals with a forecast for the remaining months into a full-year outlook.
Forecast the remaining months with a run rate on the budget.
Use FORECAST.LINEAR for a trend, and see why it misleads on seasonal sales.
topics: Why a straight line misses Diwali

modules.summary: Inputs, calculations and outputs; consistent formulas, timelines and flags; checks and error traps; and documenting and reviewing a model.

lessons.title: Inputs, calculations and outputs
lessons.summary: A model others can trust keeps every assumption in one place, works everything out in formulas that point at those inputs, and shows the answers separately. No numbers typed inside formulas; names for the key inputs.
objectives: Explain why models separate inputs, calculations and outputs.
Use a colour code that shows which cells to change.
Link calculations to inputs on another sheet, with no numbers typed inside formulas.
Name a key input and use the name in formulas.

lessons.title: Consistent formulas, timelines and flags
lessons.summary: Every row of a model should hold one formula, the same in every column. A timeline of real dates drives the model; flags of 1 and 0 switch things on and off; SUMIFS rolls months up into years.
objectives: Write one formula per row that works in every column, with no special first column.
Build a timeline with EDATE, EOMONTH and a financial-year row.
Use flags (1 or 0) with IF and AND to switch costs and revenue on and off.
Roll monthly figures up into financial years with SUMIFS.

modules.title: The three-statement model
modules.summary: Revenue and cost drivers, working capital, fixed-asset and debt schedules, the cash flow statement, and a balance sheet that balances.
modules.testInfo: Drivers, working capital, schedules, cash flow and balancing

lessons.title: Revenue and cost drivers
lessons.summary: A three-statement model forecasts the P&L, the balance sheet and the cash flow together, year by year. It starts with the P&L: revenue from a growth rate, each cost from its own driver, and EBITDA and its margin.
objectives: Explain what a three-statement model is and how the statements link.
Lay out a model with actual years followed by forecast years.
Forecast revenue from growth and each cost from its own driver.
Work out EBITDA, its margin and revenue growth a year (CAGR), and sense-check them against history.
topics: Costs: % of revenue, or their own growth

lessons.title: Working capital
lessons.summary: Profit isn’t cash: money is tied up in stock and in customers who haven’t paid, and freed by suppliers who haven’t been paid. Forecast each balance from its days, and the increase in working capital is cash the business needs to grow.
objectives: Explain why working capital ties up cash.
Work out receivable, inventory and payable days from a year’s accounts.
Forecast the balances from days, and net working capital.
Work out the increase in working capital, and what a change in days does to cash.

lessons.title: Fixed assets and debt
lessons.summary: Two schedules feed the model: the fixed-asset ‘corkscrew’ (opening + capex − depreciation = closing) and the loan corkscrew (opening + drawn − repaid = closing), with interest on the average balance.
objectives: Build a fixed-asset schedule where each year’s closing net block becomes the next year’s opening.
Forecast depreciation as a % of the opening net block.
Build a term-loan schedule with drawdowns and repayments that never exceed what’s owed.
Work out interest on the average balance, and explain why.

lessons.title: The cash flow statement
lessons.summary: The cash flow statement explains how cash changed: cash from operations (profit, plus non-cash charges, less the increase in working capital), from investing (capex) and from financing (loans and dividends). Its closing cash is the balance sheet’s cash.
objectives: Name the three sections of a cash flow statement and what goes in each.
Work out cash from operations from profit with the indirect method.
Get the signs right: cash in positive, cash out negative.
Work out the net change and closing cash, which link to the balance sheet.
topics: Signs: in is plus, out is minus

lessons.title: The balance sheet: making it balance
lessons.summary: Every balance sheet line comes from a schedule: cash from the cash flow, retained earnings from profit less dividends. If every change is in the cash flow, assets equal equity and liabilities in every year. A balance check shows when they don’t, and the size of the gap shows why.
objectives: Link each balance sheet line to its schedule, and roll retained earnings forward.
Explain why a fully linked model balances.
Add a balance check, and use the pattern of the gap to find what’s wrong.
Avoid circular references, and know what to do when one is unavoidable.

modules.title: Valuation and DCF
modules.summary: Free cash flow, the cost of capital, discounting and terminal value, and from enterprise value to a value per share.
modules.testInfo: Free cash flow, WACC, terminal value and value per share

lessons.title: Free cash flow
lessons.summary: A business is worth the cash it will produce for everyone who funds it. Free cash flow to the firm is operating profit after tax, plus depreciation, less capex and the increase in working capital: the cash left for lenders and owners together.
objectives: Explain the idea of a discounted cash flow (DCF) valuation.
Work out EBIT and the tax on it, and NOPAT.
Build free cash flow to the firm from NOPAT, depreciation, capex and working capital.
Explain why free cash flow is measured before interest and loans.
topics: Value = the cash it will produce
Free cash flow to the firm

lessons.title: The cost of capital
lessons.summary: The discount rate is the return investors could expect elsewhere for the same risk. The cost of equity comes from CAPM (risk-free rate + beta × equity risk premium), the cost of debt is after tax, and the WACC weights the two.
objectives: Explain why the discount rate is the return investors expect, not the loan rate.
Work out beta from monthly returns with SLOPE.
Work out the cost of equity with CAPM, and the after-tax cost of debt.
Combine them into the weighted average cost of capital (WACC).
topics: Why not use the loan rate?

lessons.title: Discounting and terminal value
lessons.summary: Discount each year’s free cash flow at the WACC, then add a terminal value for every year after the forecast: the final year’s cash growing for ever, discounted back. The total is the enterprise value, and the terminal value is usually most of it.
objectives: Work out discount factors and present values for each forecast year, and check them with NPV.
Work out a terminal value with the growing-for-ever (Gordon growth) formula.
Discount the terminal value and add it to get enterprise value.
Cross-check the terminal value with an exit multiple, and judge how much of the value it carries.
topics: The business doesn’t stop in year 5

lessons.title: From enterprise value to value per share
lessons.summary: Enterprise value belongs to lenders and owners together. Take off debt and add cash to get the owners’ equity value, divide by the number of shares, and then test how much the answer moves with WACC and growth.
objectives: Turn enterprise value into equity value with net debt.
Work out a value per share, and the multiples it implies.
Build a sensitivity table of value per share by WACC and terminal growth.
Explain why a valuation is a range, and how value differs from price.

modules.title: Scenarios, sensitivity and presenting
modules.summary: Scenario switches, sensitivity and tornado charts, Goal Seek and loan sizing, and presenting a model.
modules.testInfo: Scenarios, tornadoes, Goal Seek and the summary

lessons.title: Scenario switches
lessons.summary: A scenario changes several assumptions together: a base case, an upside, a downside. Keep each scenario’s inputs in a table, pick the live set with a switch, and the whole model follows.
objectives: Explain what a scenario is, and how it differs from changing one input.
Lay out a scenario table and a live column that the model reads.
Pick the live inputs with XLOOKUP, INDEX/MATCH or CHOOSE from a switch cell.
Add a drop-down to the switch, and compare scenarios side by side.
topics: A scenario table and a live column

lessons.title: Sensitivity and tornado charts
lessons.summary: Flex each assumption up and down, one at a time, and see how far the answer moves. A tornado chart ranks the assumptions by their swing, so the debate goes to the few that matter.
objectives: Flex one input at a time between a sensible low and high, and record the result.
Work out each driver’s change from the base case and its swing.
Sort the drivers by swing with SORTBY, and chart them as a tornado.
Explain what a tornado shows and what it misses.

lessons.title: Goal Seek, Solver and loan sizing
lessons.summary: Goal Seek works a model backwards: what margin justifies the investor’s price, what loan keeps the DSCR above the bank’s minimum. When the answer must meet several conditions at once, Solver takes over.
objectives: Use Goal Seek on a model to find the input that hits a target, and check it.
Size a loan from the cash available and a minimum DSCR, with PV.
Work out the DSCR each year for a chosen loan, and the lowest.
Know when Solver is needed instead of Goal Seek.

lessons.title: Presenting a model
lessons.summary: The people who decide won’t read the model. Give them one page: the answer first, the range of outcomes, what it depends on, and what you’re asking for, with numbers that update when the model does.
objectives: Write an executive summary that puts the answer first.
Build headline text that updates from the model with & and TEXT.
Compare the results with what’s on the table, such as an offer.
Choose what to show an investor and a lender, and check the model before it goes out.
topics: Compare with what’s on the table

project.title: A three-statement model and valuation for Saanjh Snacks
project.brief: Three years of Saanjh Snacks’ accounts and the founder’s plans: build a five-year model with linked P&L, balance sheet and cash flow, a debt schedule for a new factory loan, a DCF valuation, and scenarios for the lender’s meeting.
